description: We are an ambitious team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, passionate about space, science, and innovation. Our goal is to develop creative solutions to real-world challenges and compete at the global level. We are looking for motivated team members interested in programming, research, data analysis, science, and design. We value teamwork, creativity, dedication, and a willingness to learn. Together, we aim to turn ideas into impact!
summary: LIBO Health is an offline-first health monitoring prototype for astronauts on space missions. We developed a Python system that learns each astronaut’s personal baseline from signals such as heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, and sleep. It then scores new readings against that baseline and classifies the state as normal, warning, or alert. Every alert explains its cause by naming the signals that changed most, and suggests an action. This addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health when communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable, because all processing runs on board. It is important because long missions, such as travel to Mars, need systems that understand each crew member individually, avoid one-size-fits-all thresholds, and give explainable alerts the crew can trust. Our prototype demonstrates three simulated cases: normal, fatigue, and anomaly.
details:
What it does and how it works
LIBO Health monitors an astronaut’s physiological signals (heart rate, heart rate variability, SpO2, and sleep) and raises explained alerts when the astronaut’s state departs from their own normal range. First, it builds a personal baseline for each astronaut using an exponentially weighted moving average and a robust spread estimate (median absolute deviation). Second, it converts each new reading into a deviation score and combines the scores into a weighted anomaly score. Third, it classifies the state as NORMAL, WARNING, or ALERT, names the two signals that contributed most, and suggests an action, such as rest or notifying the crew medical officer.

Benefits
Thresholds come from each astronaut’s own history instead of one-size-fits-all limits. Alerts are explainable, so the crew can understand and trust them. The method uses simple statistics that can run on low-power edge hardware without a link to Earth.

Intended impact
We want to support crew health on long missions, such as travel to Mars, where communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable, by giving crews early, understandable warnings.

Tools and technologies
Python (standard library only), Google Colab to run and test the prototype, and GitHub to host the code. The prototype demonstrates three simulated cases: normal, fatigue, and anomaly. Planned hardware includes wearable sensors for heart rate, SpO2, skin temperature, and CO2.

Creativity
The system combines personal baselines, explanations for every alert, and offline operation in one lightweight design. The architecture is modular: sensors, processing, baseline engine, anomaly detector, and alert module.

Factors we considered
Offline operation, personalization for each astronaut, explainability, low power use, and safety. Alerts are advisory and point to the crew medical officer rather than giving a diagnosis. The prototype currently uses simulated data, and we plan to validate it with real and NASA open datasets.
